Comments: This patient’s quality of life is already compromised to the extent that she is dependent on others for most cares, meaning that further compromise from nephrostomy tubes would be marginal.

This patient faces a substantial risk of morbidity and mortality from evisceration and/or obstruction should he remain in a less restrictive environment, and that could be worse than the pain he experiences from being in a less restrictive environment.

This patient was already stuck with needles to obtain blood specimens for the labs that established liver injury. A peripheral IV may have been left behind from one of these draws. It’s difficult to argue that an injection in such an IV would constitute aggressive care.
This patient’s cognitive impairment is potentially reversible.

This patient was not a good candidate for a procedure (even a trans-anal alternative to rectopexy), regardless of her value profile. She probably would not be able to learn to stop straining, and such a repair would not be durable, and she would return with recurrent prolapse.
This strikes me as a treatment non-decision, but something that should be done (and was already done) in the scenario.
This patient’s age is unknown but is relevant to prognostication.

Machine availability should have been factored in at this stage. Whether a therapy is medically reasonable for an individual and who should receive the therapy among a list of individuals competing for a scarce resource are separate questions.

I do not think organ scarcity should have been factored in, as in the ECMO scenario, but it is worth noting that scarcity of transplant organs is partly a function of how choosy the transplant surgeon is. Surgeons can transplant organs that are not a very good match for the patient by counseling the patient that it’s not a very good match, and the patient may accept the organ anyway, out of a sense of desperation, especially if they’ve been turned down for transplant elsewhere (for example, because of an uncontrolled cause of organ failure). In such a case, the biggest obstacle to transplant isn’t whether the organ is a good match, or whether the patient is a good candidate, but whether the patient has insurance that will pay the surgeon lots of money.

This patient could be a candidate for EVAR which is an alternative to open repair performed variously by surgeons and interventional radiologists, depending on the hospital. If EVAR is performed by a surgeon in the given hospital, “no surgery” seems premature, but EVAR is instead performed by interventional radiologists in the given hospital, “no surgery” makes sense and the patient should be referred for that.

Quotidian. Vicissitudes. If anyone used these words in a discussion about end-of-life care with me, I would wonder whether they were thinking about their patient, or whether they were distracted by some piece of 400-year-old literature they’d recently read. I would guess that they came from extreme wealth, and I want to never talk to them again, and yet I would continue talking to them out of a feeling that I had little choice in the matter. The prospect of death is a huge cognitive load, making plain language appropriate and effective (and also less alienating).
This patient is probably not responsible for their own meals or transportation, making this part about commitment immaterial.
This patient is intubated, making conversation infeasible, even if they did not have severe brain injury.
This patient chose to wear the pendant.

Apart from any consideration of the patient’s values, a patient with a ruptured aortic aneurysm that we expect would respond to blood products should be transfused. Incidentally, this is another case where EVAR might be a possibility.

It seemed like his only real health problem was his Alzheimer’s, which was early. I have seen patients ask for an ostomy because the risk of the surgery seems lower than the risk of eventually dying from a necrotizing soft tissue infection, not to mention that it sucks having to be turned over and cleaned up after every bowel movement. I think an ostomy in this situation is the less undignified option. I am not sure this is a close call.

There is nuance here that might not addressed by the patient’s statement. When people say they don’t want to go on dialysis, they often mean they don’t want to spend many hours a day a few days a week in a dialysis chair for what might be the rest of their life, getting stuck through a possibly grotesque-appearing aneurysmal arteriovenous fistula. That is permanent dialysis, rather than the temporary dialysis proposed for this question. Months are needed to determine the extent of recovery of renal function following acute kidney injury, and whether the need for dialysis will become permanent.

A lot of patients in this age range who present with vague pain are already thinking about cancer and surgery, to the point that I assume some degree of interest in therapy simply by their decision to show up. I would get a translator (not the son) and ask her what she thought was happening, and what she was afraid of, and she would probably bring up cancer herself. I might explain that dying from untreated disease would be more distressful and painful in some ways than this surgery.

It doesn’t sound like TURP is even on the table and surgeons can’t be compelled to cut if they think it’s not warranted. In this case, it’d probably result in a patient not just dying, but dying with a little discomfort. I think that compared to SPC, TURP requires heavier anesthesia, which is risky in this patient.
I assume this refers to SPC (intervention is given as SPC vs. TURP).
It doesn’t appear that she was on oxygen when this happened. She might be having a COPD exacerbation that could be treated with antibiotics and steroids, and could go on living for years afterwards.
This patient is acutely septic. I doubt they would be offered chemoradiation or radical surgery
